content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) is a persistent condition involving inflammation and infection of the middle ear and mastoid cavity. It is characterized by ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated tympanic membrane. The primary symptoms of CSOM include persistent ear discharge and hearing loss. Systemic antibiotics are frequently used to treat CSOM, as they work by either killing or inhibiting the growth of microorganisms responsible for the infection. These antibiotics can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of systemic antibiotics in managing CSOM. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to March 16, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared systemic antibiotics (administered orally or via injection) to placebo, no treatment, or other systemic antibiotics, with a minimum follow-up period of one week. Participants included those with chronic ear discharge lasting at least two weeks, either of unknown cause or due to CSOM. Other treatments were permitted if both the treatment and control groups received them equally. The review included 18 studies involving 2,135 participants, though many studies had unclear or high risks of bias. The primary outcomes assessed were the resolution of ear discharge (or achieving a dry ear), health-related quality of life, and ear pain. Secondary outcomes included hearing, serious complications, and ototoxicity. 1. Systemic antibiotics versus no treatment/placebo: One study compared intravenous antibiotics to placebo. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether systemic antibiotics improved the resolution of ear discharge within one to two weeks (risk ratio [RR] 8.47, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.88 to 38.21; 33 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The study did not report outcomes for ear discharge resolution beyond two weeks, health-related quality of life, ear pain, or ototoxicity. Evidence for hearing and serious complications was also very uncertain. 2. Systemic antibiotics versus no treatment/placebo (both groups received topical antibiotics): Six studies were included, with five providing usable data. When oral ciprofloxacin was compared to placebo or no treatment, and both groups received ciprofloxacin ear drops, there appeared to be little or no difference in the resolution of ear discharge at one to two weeks (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.12; 390 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were available for outcomes beyond two weeks. Health-related quality of life, ear pain, serious complications, and ototoxicity were not adequately reported. 3. Systemic antibiotics versus no treatment/placebo (both groups received other background treatments): Two studies used topical antibiotics combined with steroids as background treatment. One study compared metronidazole to placebo and found very uncertain evidence regarding the resolution of ear discharge at four weeks (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.65; 40 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Another study compared co-trimoxazole to placebo and found very uncertain evidence of improved resolution of ear discharge at six weeks (RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.16; 98 participants; very low-certainty evidence). A separate study used topical antiseptics as background treatment and found no significant difference in ear discharge resolution between amoxicillin and no treatment at three to four months (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.41; 136 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Across these studies, there was no clear evidence of differences in health-related quality of life, hearing, or serious complications. Ototoxicity was also not well-reported. 4. Comparisons of different systemic antibiotics: Eight studies compared different classes of systemic antibiotics, including quinolones versus beta-lactams, lincosamides versus nitroimidazoles, and various beta-lactams against each other. The evidence was insufficient to determine whether any specific class or type of systemic antibiotic was superior in resolving ear discharge. Adverse events were poorly reported across these studies. Conclusions: The available evidence on the effectiveness of systemic antibiotics for CSOM is limited and of very low certainty. When systemic antibiotics are used alone (with or without aural toileting), it remains unclear whether they are more effective than placebo or no treatment. When added to effective interventions such as topical antibiotics, systemic antibiotics appear to provide little or no additional benefit in resolving ear discharge. There is also no clear evidence to suggest that one class of systemic antibiotic is more effective than another. Adverse effects of systemic antibiotics were not well-documented, and given the sparse evidence of their efficacy, the potential for adverse events may outweigh their use in treating CSOM.
